title: One in five ORE hopefuls have tried over six times to secure a place
html:
A survey on the impact of the Overseas Registration Exam (ORE) booking system revealed that almost one in five (19%) hopefuls had tried more than six times to book a place to sit the Part 1 examination.

The majority of those surveyed (82%) had been attempting to sit the exam for more than a year, with more than half waiting for over two years (53%). The General Dental Council (GDC) recently estimated that the waitlist for the exam sits at around 8,000.

Technical difficulties reported after recent booking windows were echoed in the survey. Respondents described endless loading (45%), error messages (35%), blank pages (31%), and forced logouts (16%).

One described the process as ‘extremely stressful and unreliable’. They said: ‘Repeated system errors, technical failures, and the lack of a fair booking process made it very difficult to secure an exam place.’

The GDC has said that it will be implementing a new portal for exams scheduled from the beginning of 2027.

‘Treated like literal guinea pigs’

Almost all of the ORE hopefuls reported a negative effect of the process on their lives. Stress, anxiety or mental-health effects were described by 93%, while 85% said major life plans were delayed, 84% reported financial strain, and 37% cited visa instability.

A candidate said: ‘Waiting for the exam has me stuck… it’s taking a toll on my family, health, and mental health.’

The results also pointed to an impact on the dental workforce. While 65% were working in dentistry but not as a dentist, 15% said they were unemployed or in full time study.

The research analysis provided to Dentistry used a small sample of 74 professionals, so may not be representative of all ORE candidates.

In October, the pass rate for September’s sitting of Part 2 of the ORE dropped by 29% on the previous one. This was the first examination under new contractual arrangements, containing ‘refreshed assessment content to reflect contemporary clinical practice’. The correct guidance for the new assessment was released on 4 August, five weeks before the exam was scheduled.

One candidate told Dentistry: ‘Many of us have spent years to just get a slot for this exam and when we finally did, we have been treated like literal guinea pigs.’

The GDC said it understood failing the exam would be disappointing for candidates, but noted that ‘analysis shows that all four components performed reliably, that examiners marked consistently, and that the pass standard was set appropriately’.

The candidate added: ‘The real victims are the students who have lost out financially and mentally, yet have had no answers forthcoming.’
